v.why: Diminishing returns: a conv on edge 5 adds less when edge 3 already has a conv.
A conv on edge 4 adds less when the direct edge 3 is already a strong conv.
A conv on edge 3 gives a smaller gain when edge 5 already provides a conv path to the output.
A strong direct conv path reduces the marginal value of a conv on edge 0.
Removing edge 5 hurts less when a strong direct conv path to the output remains.
Removing edge 4 hurts less when edge 3 already provides a strong conv path.
With no direct path, a conv on edge 5 is a more important route to the output.
If edge 5 is absent, edge 4 is a main output path, so a conv there matters more.
A skip on the direct edge matters more when the other output edges are weak or missing.
Filling an empty direct input-to-output edge with a conv adds far more than swapping one existing op for another.

raw:
Here are the 10 I kept. Most are interactions where a strong conv on the direct input-to-output edge (edge 3) or a competing output path changes how much an edit matters. The naive reading that would mislead other raters is "more convs means more capacity, so another conv always helps". I dropped the dead-node hypotheses (edges 0, 5 and so on) because they follow from structure alone.
